name: Asprosin

lead: Asprosin is a hormone released from fat tissue during fasting. In mice it tells the liver to release glucose and the brain to increase appetite, so fat-loss readers follow it as a possible appetite target, where blocking it could ease weight gain.

It is cleaved from fibrillin-1 by furin; reported receptors include OLFR734/OR4M1 in the liver and PTPRD in the brain, and antibodies against it lowered weight in mouse models. People with obesity or diabetes tend to have higher levels, while people with a rare syndrome of low asprosin are very lean.

paras: There is no product to use; interest centres on antibody-based approaches that lower it, which have been shown in mice only.
No approved product exists and no human safety data for administering or blocking it are described in the sources reviewed.

chain: Blocking it might ease weight gain
angle.text: Asprosin is a fasting hormone from fat that raises glucose and appetite in mice, so fat-loss readers follow it as a target where lowering it could mean lower intake and easier leanness. High levels track with obesity; no appearance use exists.

lead: Asprosin is a fasting-induced protein hormone cleaved from fibrillin-1 (encoded by FBN1) and released mainly from white fat. It was described in 2016 by Atul Chopra's group at Baylor College of Medicine as raising blood glucose during fasting, and in 2017 as stimulating appetite through the brain.[1][2][3]

Blood levels of asprosin are reported to be higher in people with obesity, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.[4][5] People with a rare inherited condition that lowers asprosin (marfanoid-progeroid-lipodystrophy syndrome) are very lean.[3]
Asprosin is an endogenous hormone. Antibody-based approaches that lower it in mice have been described, but no approved product exists.

paras: The discovery arose from studying two patients with marfanoid-progeroid-lipodystrophy syndrome, who had very low plasma asprosin, low insulin and extreme thinness. The 2016 Cell paper described asprosin as a glucogenic hormone acting on the liver, and a 2017 Nature Medicine paper described it as a centrally acting appetite-stimulating hormone.[1][2][3]

Asprosin is the C-terminal fragment of profibrillin-1, the precursor of the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1 encoded by FBN1 on chromosome 15. The enzyme furin cleaves it from the precursor, and white adipose tissue has the highest FBN1 expression and is the main proposed source, although skin fibroblasts, pancreatic beta cells and saliva have also been linked to it.[3] Researchers have grouped it with a small class of hormones cleaved from larger non-hormonal proteins, which one 2021 review named caudamins.[6]

subs.h: Effects in the liver and brain
paras: In the liver, asprosin is described as a fasting-induced hormone that stimulates glucose release through a cAMP pathway like the one used by glucagon.[1][3] In the brain it is reported to cross the blood-brain barrier and activate AgRP neurons while inhibiting POMC neurons, which increases appetite and, in mice, body weight.[2] More recent work reports effects on thirst through cerebellar neurons.[3]

OLFR734 was reported as the liver receptor in mice.[7] A 2019 attempt by an industry group to reproduce the glucose effect with recombinant protein was unsuccessful, which its authors attributed to possible reagent problems; later work in 2019 reproduced the effect and named OR4M1 as the receptor, and PTPRD has been reported to mediate the appetite effects.[3]

Studies report higher circulating asprosin in type 2 diabetes and glucose dysregulation, correlated with fasting glucose, triglycerides and insulin resistance.[4][5] Levels have also been reported to differ in obesity, in saliva as well as blood,[8] and to fall after bariatric surgery.[3] These are associations.

Findings in people are not uniform. A 2019 study reported lower circulating asprosin in obese children than in controls, in contrast to the higher adult levels reported elsewhere.[9] Plasma levels have been associated with sex hormone and lipid profiles in women with metabolic-related diseases, and levels are reported to be particularly high in polycystic ovary syndrome.[3][10] Studies of lifestyle change measure asprosin as an outcome: randomized trials of exercise and diet in men with metabolic syndrome or abdominal obesity, and a 12-week trial of combined aerobic-resistance training with taurine in men with obesity, have tracked changes in asprosin alongside other metabolic markers.[11][12][13]

sections.h: Where asprosin is made and how it is released
paras: White adipose tissue is the main proposed source, but FBN1 is expressed in many tissues and other contributors are likely. Human dermal fibroblasts have been linked to asprosin secretion, which suggests skin may contribute, and one 2019 report described secretion from pancreatic beta cells and islets that rose with palmitate exposure.[3] Asprosin has also been detected in saliva, which is why saliva was used in a study of its link to obesity.[3][8]

Furin cleaves profibrillin-1 in its C-terminal domain, a step also needed for fibrillin-1 to be incorporated into the extracellular matrix. The cell site of cleavage is described as largely unknown.[3] Circulating asprosin is reported to rise with fasting and fall after eating.[1]

Several receptors have been proposed and the picture has developed in steps. In 2019 a group reported that the olfactory-receptor-family protein OLFR734 (OR4M1 in humans) mediates the liver effect and reproduced the original glucose findings, after an industry group had earlier been unable to replicate two key results with recombinant asprosin, which its authors attributed to possible reagent purity issues.[3][7] In 2022 the receptor PTPRD was identified for the appetite effect, with mice lacking Ptprd showing lower appetite and leanness, and a 2023 study independently reported that asprosin raises the excitability of appetite-stimulating AgRP neurons by inhibiting SK3 potassium channels.[3] A 2026 report identified PTPRF as a glucogenic receptor in zebrafish and mice, through which asprosin reduced insulin-receptor and Akt signalling and may contribute to hepatic insulin resistance.[3]

In the brain, asprosin crosses the blood-brain barrier, activates appetite-promoting AgRP neurons and inhibits appetite-suppressing POMC neurons in the arcuate nucleus; a 2024 study further reported that it acts on cerebellar Purkinje neurons in a thirst pathway.[3]

sections.h: A new hormone class: the caudamins
paras: In 2021 Basu, Jain and Chopra proposed grouping asprosin with endostatin, endotrophin and placensin in a subclass of protein hormones called caudamins, from the Latin cauda for tail, because each is released from the C-terminal tail of a larger precursor.[6][3]

Higher circulating asprosin is reported in obese humans and mice and in people with insulin resistance; one study found particularly high levels in women with polycystic ovary syndrome, and another found that serum asprosin fell in obese patients after weight-loss surgery.[3][4][5] Because of this pattern, researchers describe asprosin-driven hunger and hepatic glucose output as possible contributors to metabolic syndrome, although results in children and some groups have run the other way.[3][9]

People who want to lose fat may follow this research for the idea that appetite hormones are a modifiable part of body composition. Asprosin itself is not something a person can raise or lower: exercise and diet intervention studies have measured it as an outcome, but no consumer product acts on it.[11][12]

No studies found testing asprosin or an asprosin blocker as an appearance treatment in humans. Registered human studies are observational, for example serum asprosin in men with acne vulgaris, and one tracked glucose-dependent asprosin dynamics in 10 people with diabetes.[14][15]
Other registered observational studies measure asprosin in periodontitis, Marfan syndrome, breast cancer and metabolic syndrome in young women, none as an appearance intervention.[16]

Because asprosin sits at the junction of glucose release and appetite, researchers have proposed it as a possible target for obesity and diabetes treatment. In 2021, anti-asprosin antibodies were reported to lower blood glucose, appetite and body weight in mouse models.[3] Whether lowering asprosin would change body composition in people has not been tested. A 2019 report from an industry group was unable to reproduce two key findings with recombinant protein, which the authors linked to possible reagent purity, while other groups reproduced the glucose effect, and the receptor assignments (OLFR734/OR4M1 in liver, PTPRD in the brain, and in 2026 PTPRF) continue to be refined.[3]

timeline.event: Romere et al. describe asprosin in Cell as a fasting-induced glucogenic hormone, after studying patients with marfanoid-progeroid-lipodystrophy syndrome at Baylor College of Medicine. [1][3]
Duerrschmid et al. report in Nature Medicine that asprosin is a centrally acting orexigenic hormone, and an MPL mouse model reproduces the human leanness. [2][3]
OLFR734 is reported as the liver receptor in mice; an industry group reports difficulty replicating key results with recombinant protein. [7][3]
Anti-asprosin antibodies reported to lower glucose, appetite and body weight in mouse models; asprosin is classed among the caudamins. [3][6]
PTPRD is identified as the orexigenic receptor in the brain. [3]
PTPRF is reported as a glucogenic receptor in zebrafish and mice. [3]
